| **SUBJECT:** | A System Design Report for Grid Enhancement Technology: Maximizing Transmission Power Delivery via Dynamic Line Rating  |

**1.0 INTRODUCTION**  
The purpose of this report is to present a detailed system-level design and implementation plan for a Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) system aimed at maximizing power delivery in existing transmission infrastructure. Traditional power transmission networks currently rely on conservative Static Line Ratings (SLR) that frequently restrict the integration of renewable energy by indicating system overloads based on "worst-case" weather assumptions \[1, 2\]. To overcome these inefficiencies, this project implements DLR technology, which utilizes fluctuating hourly models to safely unlock previously unused grid capacity based on real-time environmental conditions \[3\].

This document establishes the team's understanding of the engineering problem and details the system design, which includes data science pipelines and grid simulation environments. It also summarizes the risk reduction work completed in the lab—including N-1 contingency analysis and data anomaly detection—and outlines the test plan for the implementation phase. Finally, the report defines sub-team roles and management policies structured to successfully execute the project deliverables: a real-time UI dashboard and an economic reliability research paper.

**2.0 DESIGN PROJECT BACKGROUND**  
In traditional power systems, overhead transmission lines are governed by a Static Line Rating (SLR), which is a fixed current limit based on "worst-case" weather assumptions such as high ambient temperature, full solar radiation, and low wind speed \[1, 2\]. These extreme conditions typically occur less than 5% of the time, meaning that for the remaining 95% of the year, lines could safely carry 30-50% more power without the risk of overheating \[3\]. Consequently, clean and inexpensive renewable energy is often curtailed despite the physical wires remaining cool. To address this bottleneck, the proposed design implements Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) technology, which utilizes real-time environmental conditions and fluctuating hourly models to safely unlock previously unused grid capacity \[3\].

To ensure a successful implementation, the design must meet several critical technical specifications. Environmental accuracy is maintained by calculating real-time conductor temperature and ampacity relationships using the physical heat-balance equations defined in IEEE Standard 738 \[1\]. Furthermore, the system must preserve grid reliability by satisfying NERC Reliability Standards and N-1 Contingency Criteria to ensure redistributed loads can be safely absorbed following the loss of any single major system component \[2, 3\]. The human-machine interface will be developed as a UI dashboard following ISO 9241 standards, allowing operators to efficiently interpret and act upon dynamic capacity data \[4\]. Finally, the system will optimize dynamic rating operations to minimize energy losses in accordance with IEEE Standard P1925.1 \[5\].

The primary deliverables for this project include a simulation of the DLR system, a centralized UI dashboard for real-time monitoring and forecasting, and a research paper quantifying the economic and reliability benefits of DLR over SLR \[6, 7\]. The simulation utilizes grid telemetry, such as system load and synchrophasors, to model real-world responses, while the dashboard provides visualizations of real-time and forecasted capacity. These tools demonstrate how transitioning to time-varying ampacity can improve the operational efficiency of existing transmission infrastructure. A complete list of all relevant standards informing these deliverables is provided in Appendix A.

**3.0 SYSTEM DESIGN**  
This report proposes a modular, layered Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) system that integrates real-time environmental and grid data with predictive modeling and simulation, enabling safe, data-driven optimization of transmission line capacity beyond static limits. Our team will be implementing this system:![][image1]

**3.1 Design Concept**  
The DLR system utilizes a modular architecture composed of three primary layers: Input Data, Analysis & Modeling, and Output. Our general approach has involved developing the forecasting models and grid simulation techniques separately; these will be integrated during the implementation phase to create the final dashboard and visual methodology model.

The Input Data Layer ingests real-time weather data streams (NOAA or sensors), grid telemetry (system load, synchrophasors), and system parameters including N-1 contingencies \[2, 8\]. The Analysis & Modeling Layer employs a Python-based data science pipeline and visual model in PSS/E to perform thermal limit forecasting via regression or neural network models based on IEEE 738 \[1, 9\]. This layer also implements fail-safe protocols that default to standard static ratings if data integrity is compromised \[10\]. The Output Layer visualizes these results on the UI dashboard and summarizes findings in the economic reliability research paper \[4, 6\].

During the initial design phase, the team evaluated several alternative methodologies and data platforms before finalizing the current modular architecture. In the data collection layer, we considered utilizing third-party weather aggregators like Synoptic; however, we ultimately selected a combination of NOAA and NSRDB because of their superior data accessibility and the lack of restrictive privacy limitations that were present with other providers. For the grid simulation and visual modeling subsystem, we evaluated the feasibility of using PowerWorld. While PowerWorld provides strong visualization capabilities, we chose PSS/E because it offers more sophisticated tools for modeling time-varying dynamic data and provides a robust Python API. This seamless integration with Python is essential for our Analysis and Modeling layer, as it allows the data science pipeline to automate the injection of forecasted ampacity limits directly into the load flow environment to verify real-time grid stability.

**3.2 Risk Reduction**  
Extensive research and lab testing have been conducted to mitigate the risks associated with pushing transmission lines closer to their physical thermal limits. We examined the following factors:

**N-1 Contingency Analysis:** We utilized PSS/E to ensure the grid remains resilient against the loss of any single major component, including transmission lines and shunt capacitor banks. For each contingency case, the simulation checks for thermal limit violations on remaining lines and bus voltage deviations outside acceptable bounds following a contingency. Results are evaluated against NERC reliability standards to confirm the system operates within safe margins under all screened scenarios \[2, 3, 10\].

**Reactive Power Exhaustion:** To mitigate the technical risks associated with our Dynamic Line Rating implementation, our design team spearheaded a series of steady-state load flow simulations using PSS/E to investigate generator reactive power exhaustion. As real power transfer increases across the grid, generators must supply additional reactive power to maintain voltage stability. During testing, we ramped up power transfer on the DLR-equipped line to its maximum rating and monitored generator output reports to identify any units reaching their maximum reactive thresholds. Our results confirmed that once a generator hits its reactive power limit, it loses the ability to regulate voltage, causing the bus to transition from a PV (source) bus to a PQ (load) bus and risking system-wide instability. Consequently, we determined that implementing DLR on critical lines must be paired with the installation of static reactive support, such as switched shunt capacitor banks, at the receiving end to ensure generators do not exhaust their reactive reserves \[10\].

**Voltage Stability:** We verified that pushing a line to its DLR limit increases reactive power losses, potentially leading to voltage collapse. To quantify this risk, we used our PSS/E network model to run contingency analyses and generate PV curves for the critical load buses. Reactive power demand increases non-linearly as line loading approaches thermal limits, compressing voltage stability margins at receiving end buses. Our simulations clearly showed that the resulting surge in reactive power losses rapidly depletes available reactive reserves, pushing the system dangerously close to the point of instability. This confirms that system operators cannot safely rely on thermal constraints alone when maximizing line utilization. Consequently, our mitigation rule requires the dispatched capacity to be the minimum of the DLR thermal limit and the voltage stability limit, ensuring that ampacity increases never compromise bus voltage integrity \[3\].

**Data Integrity:** To mitigate the risk of failures caused by interrupted telemetry, communication loss, or corrupted sensor inputs, we developed a machine learning–based anomaly detection model to continuously validate incoming data streams before they are used in DLR calculations. The model is currently being trained and tuned on historical ambient weather and operating datasets to learn normal patterns for variables such as wind speed, conductor temperature, solar irradiance, and load behavior under expected conditions. By comparing real-time inputs against these learned baselines, the system can identify anomalous data as it occurs, allowing it to immediately revert to the conservative static line rating, ensuring thermal limits are not exceeded during periods of degraded data quality. Alerts are also generated for operators so maintenance or sensor troubleshooting can be performed promptly, improving long-term reliability and trust in the DLR platform \[11\].

**DLR Pipeline Validation:** To ensure the forecasting model produces reliable ampacity outputs, we have implemented several safeguards within the Python-based processing pipeline. A key component of this validation is a dimensional analysis module that explicitly tracks and verifies units throughout the calculation pipeline. This guarantees that values are represented as expected at each stage before any conclusion is drawn from them. This is validated by running test cases with intentionally introduced unit errors, such as passing a value in kW where MW is expected, and confirming the module catches and flags each one.

**Weather Data and Transmission Corridor Mapping:** We developed a spatial pipeline that defines transmission line corridors using known substation endpoints. Rather than treating a line as a single point, the pipeline discretizes the corridor into multiple geographic points along the route, each assigned its own weather data, to better capture spatial variability. Weather inputs are sourced from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) for wind speed and direction and the National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) for solar irradiance and ambient temperature. At each discrete point, the IEEE 738 heat balance equation is applied to compute a local ampacity value. The corridor-level DLR is then taken as the minimum ampacity across all points, identifying the true bottleneck segment of the line. Currently, the pipeline generates transmission corridors using synthetically connected substation coordinates as a development and validation environment, allowing the team to confirm that the IEEE 738 calculations, weather data ingestion, and minimum ampacity logic run properly before introducing real-world geometric complexity. During the implementation phase, this will be replaced with actual transmission line geometry that traces the true conductor path. 

**3.3 Test Plan**  
During the implementation phase, the team will execute a tiered testing strategy to confirm the design works as expected across each subsystem before full system integration.

**Data Science Pipeline:** Known-value validation will run the analysis pipeline on historical datasets with established correct outputs to confirm the IEEE 738 thermal calculations produce reliable ampacity results \[9\]. The test passes if the model produced ampacity outputs within an acceptable margin of the known historical values.

The dimensional analysis module will be tested by intentionally introducing unit errors throughout the pipeline and confirming every error is caught and flagged before propagating into outputs. The module is functional when it achieves 100% detection rate across all injected unit error test cases.

The anomaly detection model will be validated by injecting corrupted or out-of-range values into the weather and operating data streams, such as sudden temperature spikes or impossible wind speeds, and confirming the system correctly identifies them as anomalous and immediately reverse to the static line rating \[11\]. All injected anomalies must be correctly flagged with no false positives on clean data, and automatic fallback to SLR must be confirmed upon detection.

The transmission corridor and weather data pipeline will be validated by running the full spatial pipeline on a synthetic corridor and confirming that NOAA and NSRDB data is correctly ingested, assigned to each corridor point, and fed into the IEEE 738 heat balance calculator \[4\]. The minimum ampacity logic will be verified by artificially cooling one corridor segment and confirming the system correctly identified it as the bottleneck. Validation is confirmed when ampacity is correctly computed at all corridor points and the corridor-level DLR reflects the true minimum segment. Once integration testing of NOAA and NSRDB sources is complete, the pipeline will be rerun on actual ERCOT transmission data to confirm real-world results are reasonable and consistent with published SLR values for those lines. 

**Power Systems Subsystem:** N-1 contingency cases will be run in PSS/E across all major system components, checking that no thermal or voltage violations occur following any single component loss. The design meets this requirement if all post-contingency flows remain within DLR ampacity limits and all bus voltages remain within NERC-compliant bounds \[2, 3, 10\].

Reactive power exhaustion will be tested by ramping power transfer on the DLR equipped line to its maximum rating and monitoring generator reactive output reports to confirm no units reach their maximum reactive thresholds under normal operating conditions. A PV to PQ bus transition on any generator constitutes a test failure, as this indicates the generator has lost its ability to regulate voltage and the system is at risk of instability. In these cases, the test will verify that the switched shunt capacitor banks installed at the receiving end supply sufficient reactive support to prevent any generator from reaching its reactive limit. Acceptable conditions require no PV to PQ transitions and stable bus voltages maintained throughout the full DLR operating range.

PV curves will be generated for critical load buses to confirm that voltage stability margins remain acceptable at DLR thermal limits. Results are acceptable when the dispatched capacity never exceeds the voltage stability limit, consistent with the minimum dispatch rule established in Section 3.2 \[3\].

**UI Dashboard:** The dashboard will be tested by feeding it live pipeline outputs and confirming that DLR values, anomaly flags, and fallback status indicators update correctly in real time. A usability review will evaluate the interface against ISO 9241 requirements, focusing on clarity of alerts and operator response time to flagged conditions \[4\]. The dashboard is considered functional when operators can correctly interpret dynamic ratings and system alerts without additional guidance, and all pipeline outputs are accurately reflected in real time.

**Full System Integration:** End-to-end integration testing will connect the Data Science pipeline, PSS/E simulation, and UI dashboard into a single workflow using a live data stream. The test will confirm that a change in weather input propagates correctly through IEEE 738 calculation, updates the corridor ampacity, triggers appropriate contingency checks, and displays the updated rating on the dashboard within the trusted duration refresh window. The system is considered fully integrated when data flows end-to-end flow with no unit errors, no undetected anomalies, and dashboard outputs consistent with pipeline calculations.

**APPENDIX A: RELEVANT STANDARDS**

1. **IEEE Standard 738 \- Standard for Calculating the Current-Temperature Relationship of Bare Overhead Conductors**  
   A numerical method by which the core and surface temperatures of a bare overhead conductor are related to the steady or time-varying electrical current and weather conditions is described in this standard. Contents discussed also include how this method may be used to determine the conductor’s current for a corresponding conductor temperature limit. Please note the content in this standard does not recommend suitable weather conditions or conductor parameters for use in line rating calculations \[1\].  
2. **NERC Reliability Standards \- North American Electric Reliability Corporation**  
   NERC Reliability Standards establish mandatory requirements for the planning the operation of the bulk electric power system across North America. This project complies with NERC standards to ensure that the DLR simulation meets transmission reliability requirements, including contingency planning criteria that govern how the system must perform under abnormal operation conditions \[2\].   
3. **N-1 Contingency Criteria**  
   The N-1 Contingency Criterion requires that the bulk power system remain within thermal, voltage, and stability limits following the sudden loss of any single system component. The Power Systems team will evaluate whether transmission lines operating under dynamic ratings satisfy N-1 criteria, ensuring redistributed loads can be safely absorbed without violating limits or compromising system reliability \[3\].  
4. **ISO 9241 \- Ergonomics of Human-System Interaction**  
   ISO 9241 establishes “requirements and recommendations for human-centered design principles applied throughout the development lifecycles of interactive computer-based systems.” For this project, it guides the design of the UI dashboard to ensure that grid operators can efficiently interpret dynamic line rating data and navigate system alerts. By following this standard, the dashboard will prioritize clarity, consistency, and usability, reducing the likelihood of operator error in time-sensitive situations \[4\].  
5. **IEEE Standard P1925.1/D1.1 \- Guide for Energy Efficiency in Dynamic Line Rating Systems**  
   This standard specifies an energy-efficient, rate 1 and modulation adaptive transmission system designed for the deployment of mixed line rates in optical networks. It introduces the transmission system and provides mechanisms to optimally configure the line rate to efficiently accommodate varying traffic loads while reducing the power consumption \[5\].  
6. **IEEE Standard C37.118 \- Standard for Synchrophasor Measurements for Power Systems**  
   IEEE C37.118 establishes measurement definitions and compliance requirements for synchrophasor measurements, frequency, and rate of change of frequency (ROCOF) under varying power systems operating conditions. It specifies time synchronization and accuracy requirements, which are critical for ensuring that real-time data fed into the DLR system reflects true line conditions \[8\].  
7. **IEEE Standard C37.116 \- Guide for Protective Relay Applications to Transmission Lines Series Capacitor Banks**  
   The application of protective relays on transmission-line series capacitor banks is covered. Ample discussion of the protection and control issues related to series capacitor bank installations is provided to the reader. Specific examples related to protective functions and testing procedures are provided \[10\].  
8. **IEEE Standard 1815 \- Standard for Electric Power Systems Communications \- Distributed Network Protocol (DNP3)**  
   This document specifies the standard approach for mapping between IEEE Std 1815™ \[Distributed Network Protocol (DNP3)\] and IEC 61850 (Communications Networks and Systems for Power Utility Automation). Two primary use cases are addressed: a) mapping between an IEEE 1815-based master and an IEC 61850-based remote site and b) mapping between an IEC 61850-based master and an IEEE 1815-based remote site. Mapping aspects included in the standard are: conceptual architecture; general mapping requirements; the mapping of Common Data Classes, Constructed Attribute Classes and Abstract Communication Service Interface (ACSI); cyber security requirements, the architecture of a gateway used for translation and requirements for embedding mapping configuration information into IEC 61850 System Configuration Description Language (SCL) and DNP3 Device Profile. This standard addresses a selection of features, data classes, and services of the two standards \[11\].
